extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and researchers seeking an overview of human rights in Zimbabwe
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia country-profile article summarising reported human-rights conditions, legal framework, notable incidents, and international assessments related to Zimbabwe. It compiles allegations, laws used, case examples, and historical Freedom House ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core human rights allegedly violated
rubrics_metrics.description: According to human rights organisations such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch the government of Zimbabwe violates the rights to shelter, food, freedom of movement and residence, freedom of assembly and the protection of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statement functions as a summary criterion for assessing the state's overall compliance with basic economic, social and civil rights. Examples and later sections document specific ways these rights have been undermined (e.g., food shortages, forced removals, restrictions on movement and assembly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Police repression and law enforcement abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a widespread consensus among human rights organisations that systematic violations of the right of personal freedom and integrity are frequent in Zimbabwe, especially towards suspected members of the political opposition. The violations ... include assaults, torture, death threats, kidnappings and unlawful arrests and detentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports evaluation of state behavior by looking for patterns of assault/torture/kidnapping/unlawful detention by police and security services. The article provides multiple case examples (e.g., MDC rally crackdowns, abduction/murder of journalist Edward Chikombo, trade unionists beaten at Matapi police station, detention and beatings of student activist Promise Mkwanazi). Also cites NGO tallies (e.g., Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum statistics from 2001–2006).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of assembly (legal and practical restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Zimbabwe the freedom of assembly is severely restricted by law. The legal framework is further stretched in practice, with law enforcement closely monitoring opposition demonstrations and public gatherings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether laws (notably the Public Order and Security Act (POSA) and the Miscellaneous Offences Act (MOA)) are used to disrupt peaceful demonstrations, justify arrests, or enable holding activists longer than legally allowed. Examples: arrests and beatings of demonstrators, denial of rights at rallies, and government monitoring of assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of expression and press freedom; access to information
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom House finds that Zimbabwe's freedom of expression and freedom of the press has deteriorated. The 2002 Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA) requires journalists and media companies to register with the government-controlled Media and Information Commission (MIC) and gives the government powers to deny people the right to work as journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate existence and use of accreditation/registration laws (AIPPA), criminal penalties for unaccredited journalism (up to two years' imprisonment after 2005 amendment), closure of oppositional media, state control of broadcast media and major dailies, denial of visas/accreditation to foreign journalists, monitoring of e-mail, and prosecution for publishing 'inaccurate' information. Examples include closures of newspapers, intimidation, and deportation threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral integrity: free and fair elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The general consensus is that these and prior elections in Zimbabwe have not been free and fair, with widespread electoral fraud. Candidates and supporters of the opposition party, MDC, have been restricted from campaigning openly in some areas, and have faced harassment, violence and intimidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should look for indicators such as voter intimidation at polling stations, manipulation of voter rolls/redistricting, turning voters away (e.g., due to poorly publicised redistricting), vote buying (government food stocks offered in exchange for votes), biased media coverage, and discrepancies in vote reporting that favour the ruling party. The 2008 elections and run-off violence are cited as concrete examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of torture and cruel/inhuman treatment (including alleged torture camps)
rubrics_metrics.description: There have been allegations of torture including severe beatings, sexual assault and dog mauling; it was alleged that Zimbabwe's security forces had a torture camp in the Marange diamond fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reports (NGOs, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch) documenting methods and locations of torture, specific cases (e.g., Amnesty reporting torture/sexual assault of activists Joana Mamombe, Cecilia Chimbiri, Netsai Marova), and corroborating details to evaluate compliance with absolute prohibition on torture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes against humanity and mass atrocities allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been widespread reports of egregious crimes against humanity by the Mugabe government between 1980 and 2017. Scholars and experts have claimed there was 'clear evidence that Mugabe was guilty of crimes against humanity' and sufficient evidence to bring charges before the International Criminal Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria include documented large-scale killings (e.g., Gukurahundi, Fifth Brigade actions), estimates of death tolls, expert scholarly assessments, and calls for independent inquiries or international prosecutions. The article cites alleged massacres (e.g., Chikurubi Prison) and disputed death-toll estimates as material evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of due process, legal assistance and inhumane detention conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Detainees have been denied medical and juridical assistance, detained for days without charge, repeatedly stripped, shackled and beaten; detention cells described as of inhuman conditions and poor sanitary standards with non-flushing toilets and little air ventilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether arrests are followed by prompt charges, access to legal representation and medical care, humane detention conditions, and whether detainees are held beyond legally allowed limits. Specific cited cases (trade unionists, student activists) illustrate these abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination against women (sexism) and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are disadvantaged in Zimbabwe, with economic dependency and social norms preventing them from combating sex discrimination. Despite legal prohibitions, customs such as forced marriage are still in place. Domestic violence against women is a serious problem. Labour legislation prohibits sexual harassment in the workplace, but such harassment is common and generally not prosecuted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both legal protections on the books (rights to property, inheritance, divorce; labour law prohibitions) and the gap in implementation: prevalence of forced marriage, domestic violence, lack of prosecution for sexual harassment, and lack of awareness of rights among women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people
rubrics_metrics.description: Common law prevents homosexual men, and to a lesser extent homosexual women, from fully expressing their sexual orientation. The criminal code has been amended to define sodomy to include 'any act involving physical contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person to be an indecent act.' Same-sex sexual activity — penalty: 14 years imprisonment with fines. Constitutional ban on same-sex marriage since 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure legal status (criminalisation, sodomy definitions, penalties), gaps in anti-discrimination protections (employment, goods and services), bans (marriage), and practical consequences (social stigma, prosecutions). The article lists multiple indicators (penalties, lack of rights, service restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of legislation and administrative power to suppress dissent (POSA, MOA, AIPPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws such as the Public Order and Security Act (POSA), the Miscellaneous Offences Act (MOA) and the 2002 Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA) are used to violently disrupt peaceful demonstrations, criminalise journalism, and justify arrests of civil society activists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating civic space, examine how broadly worded public-order and information laws are applied, whether they enable arbitrary arrests or accreditation control, and whether amendments increase penalties or empower state commissions to deny journalistic work. The article gives examples of these laws' application in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: External measurements: Freedom House 'Freedom in the World' rating (1–7 scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following is Zimbabwe's ratings since 1972 in the Freedom in the World reports, published annually by Freedom House rated on a scale from 1 (most free) to 7 (least free). The table lists yearly political rights and civil liberties scores and overall status (Not free/Partly free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Freedom House annual numeric scores and statuses as a standardized metric to compare political rights and civil liberties over time. The article provides the historical series as context for longitudinal assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government narrative and official responses to allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: The government of Zimbabwe has generally responded to accusations of human rights violations from Western countries by counter-accusals of colonial attitudes and hypocrisy, claiming that countries such as the United Kingdom and the United States are guilty of similar or worse transgressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the state's official statements, denials, and counter-accusations as part of assessing accountability and the political context. The article cites speeches (e.g., Patrick Chinamasa at the UN Human Rights Council) asserting respect for human rights while accusing NGOs of undermining sovereignty.
